messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Fashion Designer
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 77

He is a forty-nine-year-old man with the quiet, deliberate posture of someone who has spent decades learning to see what others miss. In the first session, he sits forward on the chair, hands resting on his knees, palms open—a gesture that seems both inviting and rehearsed. His clothes are impeccably cut, charcoal gray, the fabric soft and unstructured. He is a fashion designer, and he speaks of his work the way a musician speaks of silence: with reverence, and with loss.

The story begins two years ago, in late October. He was in the final push before a runway show in Paris, working eighteen-hour days in his studio, surrounded by swatches of silk and organza, by pinned muslins and rolls of pattern paper. His wife, a curator at a contemporary art museum, had driven to a gallery opening in the countryside. On the way back, a driver ran a red light. She was airlifted to a trauma center with a severe traumatic brain injury, multiple fractures, and internal bleeding.

He remembers the phone call. He was holding a length of cobalt-blue crepe de chine when his assistant handed him the phone. The voice on the line told him there had been an accident. He drove to the hospital with the piece of fabric still in his coat pocket. He does not know why he kept it. He sat in the waiting room for eleven hours, rubbing the silk between his thumb and forefinger until the edge frayed. When the surgeon finally came out, he could not understand the words. He only understood the expression on the surgeon’s face.

She survived. She is home now, but the person who lives in their house is not the person he married. She has memory gaps, emotional lability, aphasia that comes and goes like weather. She does not remember the accident at all, which he finds both merciful and unbearable. He wishes she could remember so that she could share the weight. Instead, he carries it alone.

Now, in the present, his life has contracted. He has not designed a full collection in eighteen months. He tried, six months after the crash, to sketch a women’s coat. He drew the lapel, the shoulder, the dart. Then he saw the shape of a cervical collar, the curve of a neck brace, and he threw the sketchbook across the room. He cannot look at medical dramas on television. He cannot drive past the intersection where it happened; he takes a three-mile detour every time he leaves the house. His assistant now brings fabric swatches to his home, but even there, the textures betray him. Velvet reminds him of the blanket a nurse placed over his wife’s legs. Linen reminds him of the curtains in the ICU cubicle. He once loved the way a fabric could hold light. Now light feels like a thing that can be taken away.

He sleeps in a separate bedroom because his wife’s nightmares wake him. But his own nightmares are worse. In the dream, he is always arriving at the hospital a few minutes earlier. He is standing at the door of the trauma bay, and he can see the car, except the car is made of things he knows: a zipper, a button, a seam. He wakes with his heart pounding, convinced he has failed her by not being there, by not preventing it, by being in love with a piece of fabric when she needed him.

He has become hypervigilant. On the rare occasions he goes out—to a gallery opening, a dinner—he scans every room for exits, for signs of danger. He checks his phone compulsively, even when there is no message. He has started to notice that his hands tremble when he hears a sudden loud noise, like a car horn or a door slamming. He used to enjoy those sounds, the pulse of the city. Now they are sirens.

His marriage is a landscape of silence and apologies. He wants to be present for her, but he finds himself irritable, distant. She asks him about his work, and he says “fine” because the truth would be too much. He feels guilty for his own grief, because she is the one who suffered, and yet he cannot stop replaying that night. He watches her struggle to find a word, and he sees the crash. He hears her laugh at something on television, and he sees the surgeon’s face.

He has stopped going to the studio. The machines are still there, the cutting table, the bolts of fabric gathering dust. He tells himself he will go back soon. But every time he thinks about it, he feels a tightness in his chest, a cold that starts in his stomach and spreads to his legs. He sits in his home office, surrounded by sketches he can no longer finish, and he thinks: I used to know how to make beautiful things. Now I only know how to wait.
